candidates.evidence_text: Families 'devastated' as Stretford school closure announced - BBC News Image caption, Sue Green says she does not want to move her daughter before the school closes By Haider Saleem Reporting from Greater Manchester Published 23 October 2026 Families have been left "absolutely devastated" by a decision to close a primary school in Greater Manchester. St Teresa's RC Primary School in Firwsood, Trafford, will close down in August 2027. One mother told the BBC she feared she might not be able to get a place for her daughter at another local Roman Catholic school. The council said falling pupil numbers had made the school's finances unsustainable. St Teresa's is a state-funded school and its budget is managed by its governing body. The Roman Catholic Diocese of Salford owns the site and has a role in its governance, but Trafford Council oversees its finances, and made the decision to close it. Council documents show St Teresa's had 109 pupils in July. Of those, 21 had since left to attend secondary school, while 51 secured places at other primary schools for September. With two new reception pupils joining, the school had 39 children on its roll by the time of the council's October report. The council estimated that 24 pupils would need to move to another primary school when St Teresa's closes, with the remaining 15 moving on to secondary school. Image caption, Helen fears she may struggle to secure a place at another nearby Catholic school for her daughter Parents and teachers said they believed the proposed closure encouraged families to move their children before councillors had reached a final decision. The council acknowledged some families had moved early but said parents were entitled to seek places elsewhere at any time. A spokesperson said the council could not guarantee a child a place at a particular school, because admissions decisions depended on each school's arrangements, but added that three primary schools within 1 mile (1.6km) of St Teresa's had vacancies, along with two Catholic schools within 1.5 miles (2.4km). Council figures show more than 50 pupils secured places at other primary schools before the decision, leaving just 39 on its roll. Helen Fitzpatrick, whose daughter goes to the school, said families were "absolutely devastated" by the decision, announced on Monday. The 39-year-old, who has helped organise a campaign against the closure, said she had contacted nearby St Ann's RC Primary School but was told it could not guarantee a place for September 2027. Although a place was available when she asked, she said she would have had to accept it immediately and her daughter was not "ready to leave St Teresa's until it closes". She said she also feared her child could "get lost in the crowd" at a larger school. Image caption, Cameron, whose two daughters attend St Teresa's, thinks more could have been done to save the school Another parent, Sue Green, said she faced a similar dilemma over her five-year-old daughter. Her three children have attended St Teresa's over the past 12 years. She said she had been told she would have to wait until July to apply for a September 2027 place, unless she transferred her daughter immediately. She said she did not want to disrupt he daughter's education by moving her before the school closed. "It's just so unfair," she said. Cameron Kennedy, who has two daughters aged nine and five, said he felt more could have been done to save the school. "I don't really think it was given much of a chance," the 41-year-old said. Image caption, The school is due to close in August 2027 St Teresa's deficit stood at almost £196,000 at the end of 2025-26 and could exceed £1m by 2029-30 if the school remains open. The council spokesperson said the authority "had to make the difficult decision to close St Teresa's because of the significant fall in numbers of children over several years". They said the council had worked with the school on its finances and explored alternatives, but was unable to identify a sustainable recovery plan. "Closure is always a last resort," they added. The decision has also left long-serving teachers facing an uncertain future. Tracy Dawson, who has worked at St Teresa's for 25 years, said she had regarded it as the school where she would spend the rest of her career. candidates.evidence_text: A teenager who wrote his own terrorism manifesto and is accused of stirring up racial hatred against Jewish people and foreigners has pleaded guilty to 12 terrorism offences Damien Woolfenden, 18, formerly of Bury, admitted posting Christchurch attacker Brenton Tarrant's live-streamed video of the 2019 killings on to the self-described "pro-white" platform White Pilled TV He also posted the manifesto of far-right terrorist Andres Breivik, who killed 77 people in two attacks in Norway in 2011, on to a Telegram group Woolfenden pleaded guilty to other charges of disseminating terrorist material, as well as possessing publications useful for terrorism, including the Anarchist's Cookbook During the hearing at the Old Bailey it emerged that Woolfenden had written his own terrorist manifesto in which he said he would "wait until after an election in 2028" Remanding the 18-year-old in custody for pre-sentence reports to be compiled, Judge Cheema Grubb said she had seen "mindset material by the defendant which seems to advocate violence against groups"

candidates.lead: The Grade II-listed Marble Arch has been serving pints on Manchester's Rochdale Road since 1888
candidates.evidence_text: Plans for 17-storey tower by historical Marble Arch pub rejected - BBC News Image source, LDRS Image caption, Plans for the 17-storey tower have prompted concerns over the Marble Arch's future By Declan Carey Local Democracy Reporting Service Published 23 October 2026 Plans for a 17-storey tower block next to a historical Manchester pub have been rejected by councillors. Developer The McGoff Group had applied to build 153 flats beside the Grade II-listed Marble Arch on Rochdale Road, which has been serving customers since 1888. The company said the scheme would deliver much-needed city centre housing and help regenerate the area. But the pub's owners argued the development threatened its future, and Manchester City Council's planning committee voted to refuse the application. In its objection, the pub said the 17-storey building would be "overbearing and oppressive" and would harm the setting of the pub. Councillors also raised concerns about the impact of the development on the Marble Arch and the lack of affordable housing in the scheme. Councillor Jon-Connor Lyons said he was "deeply concerned" about the effect on "one of Manchester's distinctive and much-loved historic pubs". A member of staff told the Local Democracy Reporting Service : "We get tourists coming from all over the world who are sent here. "We have generations of families drinking here, dads and grandads and sons. You don't get places like this anymore and it's something we want to keep going." candidates.evidence_text: Two women who were preyed upon by serving police officers they trusted have described their ordeals and why they decided to speak out Naomi Meadows was raped by a detective she met online in Devon, while Catherine Dobson was subjected to years of coercive and controlling behaviour by a Lancashire police officer who worked in a sexual offences unit Catherine said: "He used his job, he used his power and he abused the badge. The women waived their right to anonymity to tell their harrowing stories as part of a BBC investigation that uncovered more than 1,200 domestic abuse allegations made in three years against police officers and special constables across England and Wales Professional standards investigations were opened into allegations including rape, sexual assault, grievous bodily harm, stalking and serious violence Most cases were discontinued, subjected to no further action or dropped because of a lack of evidence or victims withdrawing their complaints

candidates.evidence_text: Social media is in part behind a spate of recent "racially or religiously motivated" attacks on houses in multiple occupation (HMOs) across Greater Manchester, a senior police officer has said Greater Manchester Police said there had been 46 properties damaged across the city region since 5 October, including in Salford, Tameside and Stockport Ch Sup Marcus Noden said footage of criminal damage was being shared widely "followed by comments and discussions", and people were using social media to "push the message out across different areas" He warned people to stop the attacks, which he said were "unlawful, reckless and putting lives at risk" As an investigation into the run of criminal damage continues, a 33-year-old man was arrested on Wednesday morning on suspicion of conspiracy to commit criminal damage and remained in custody for questioning The damage was to HMOs or properties that were mistaken for HMOs

candidates.lead: Social workers were told children were in "great danger" days before a fatal fire, an inquest hears
candidates.evidence_text: Social workers received an anonymous tip-off that children were in "great danger" days before they were murdered in an arson attack, an inquest heard Demi Pearson, 14, her brother, Brandon, eight, and sisters, Lacie, seven, and Lia, three, died after petrol bombs were thrown into their home on Jackson Street, Walkden, Salford, in the early hours of December 11, 2017 Their mother Michelle Pearson, 37, died almost two years later after suffering severe burns A joint inquest into their deaths, now in its third week, is being heard at Bolton Coroners' Court and on Wednesday it heard of social services involvement with the family The hearing was told on 29 November, 2017, less than two weeks before the fatal attack, the social services department at Salford City Council received an anonymous call The caller said: "The children are in a really unsafe environment and in great danger."

english_fact_card.what_happened: An inquest heard that social workers received an anonymous tip-off that children were in 'great danger' days before they were murdered in an arson attack. Demi Pearson, 14, Brandon, 8, Lacie, 7, and Lia, 3, died after petrol bombs were thrown into their home on Jackson Street, Walkden, Salford, on 11 December 2017. Their mother Michelle Pearson, 37, died almost two years later from severe burns. The joint inquest is in its third week at Bolton Coroners' Court.
english_fact_card.where: Bolton Coroners' Court; the fire occurred on Jackson Street, Walkden, Salford.
english_fact_card.when: Inquest hearing on 21 October 2026; tip-off was on 29 November 2017; fire on 11 December 2017.
english_fact_card.who_affected: The Pearson family and the wider community; social services and Salford City Council are under scrutiny.
english_fact_card.why_now: The inquest is ongoing and revealing new details about the lead-up to the fatal fire.
english_fact_card.reader_value: The case highlights potential failures in child protection and is of significant public interest.

The women waived their right to anonymity to tell their harrowing stories as part of a BBC investigation that uncovered more than 1,200 domestic abuse allegations made in three years against police officers and special constables across England and Wales Professional standards investigations were opened into allegations including rape, sexual assault, grievous bodily harm, stalking and serious violence Most cases were discontinued, subjected to no further action or dropped because of a lack of evidence or victims withdrawing their complaints

candidates.evidence_text: More than 100 hopefuls descended on a Manchester cafe to apply for a part-time barista role in person after what the manager described as a "whirlwind" of interest for previous jobs Applicants were invited to attend the Fig & Sparrow in the city's Northern Quarter to present their CVs rather than simply apply online after more than 400 emails were received for a vacancy earlier in the year General manager Luke Taylor, 32, said he wanted to meet people face-to-face and added: "It shows how the job market is at the minute "People are turning up on a random Tuesday in a cafe that they have probably never been to, hoping for the best." It follows a recent warning from Prime Minister Andy Burnham that the UK faces an "economic catastrophe" due to the nearly one million young people remaining without work, education or training This week, the government is expected to announce plans aimed at giving young people more opportunities

candidates.evidence_text: In recent weeks, a spate of vandalism has seen up to 50 houses attacked in Salford and neighbouring areas of Greater Manchester Windows have been smashed, doors ripped from their hinges and walls daubed with graffiti opposing "HMOs" The term HMO is not widely known outside housing and planning circles. It stands for "House in Multiple Occupation" and refers to properties where three or more unrelated people live, usually with separate bedrooms but shared facilities such as kitchens and bathrooms While HMOs are often associated with students and young professionals, they can also provide accommodation for people leaving prison, those recovering from drug or alcohol problems, and refugees Police in Salford have said they believe that the recent spate of vandalism aimed at HMOs in the area has been "racially or religiously motivated" The term HMO was formalised in the Housing Act 1985. candidates.evidence_text: Trafford Trafford pub wanted 'nightclub hours', but the plan backfired in a way they weren't expecting Bosses were told 'that's the risk' after residents complained about ‘domestics’ and ‘urination' Add to preferred sources Comments News Hannah Richar Bosses at a Trafford pub have been told ‘that’s the risk’ as they lost a bid to stay open later - and instead had new restrictions slapped on their licence Garrick’s Head, in Moorside Road, Flixton, wanted to extend its opening hours to 12.30am on Sundays through Thursdays, 1.30am on Fridays and Saturdays and 2.30am around bank holidays. It also wanted permission to be able to extend opening hours until 2am on up to 20 days each yea But following interventions from neighbours, Trafford council’s licensing committee opted instead to impose a number of new conditions on the pub. Those conditions had been intended by the applicant as safeguards had the extended hours been allowed When the agent speaking on behalf of Garrick's Head questioned the decision, saying the pub had come away with ‘no extra hours’ but ‘more restrictions’, she was told by officers that is ‘the risk that you run when you apply for a variation of the licence’ The decision followed around an hour of representations from residents who labelled the dubbed the proposed changes as ‘nightclub hours’ and said they had been suffering for years. Complaints included disturbed sleep, fights in the street, public urination and littering

candidates.evidence_text: Courts Two Iranian men in court accused of terrorism offences over alleged plot to target Manchester's Jewish community Rahman Salehi and Salam Ahmadyan appeared in court Add to preferred sources News Andrew Bardsley Court reporter 14:54, 23 Oct 2026 Two Iranian men have appeared in court accused of terrorism offences following an alleged bomb plot to target Manchester's Jewish community The Jewish Museum and Heaton Park Synagogue were allegedly targets identified by Rahman Salehi, 34, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36. The pair, who arrived in the UK by small boat, are accused of trying to acquire components to assemble a homemade explosive device Both men appeared at the Old Bailey in London this afternoon (October 23). Prosecutors allege that the pair were engaging in conduct in preparation for acts of terrorism against the Jewish community in Greater Manchester They were arrested on Newton Street in the Northern Quarter, on September 20, as thousands of British Jews prepared to celebrate the annual occasion. It is alleged that the two men were in contact with an overseas third party who may be in Iran in relation to the plot, Counter Te The defendants appeared in court by video link. They were not asked to enter pleas to the charges they face during the 22 minute hearing, which was presided over by Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb

The former Tavern Fayre at Hunger Hill, which was previously known as The Tavern On The Hill, is at the centre of the proposals put forward this week by EG on The proposed development would knock down the current pub building and replace it with a petrol filling station and retail shop, eight car-fuelling positions, two dedicated HGV fuelling lanes, four super-rapid electric-vehicle charging bays (Tesla Supercharger), a drive-through c The Tavern on Wigan Road was refurbished in the mid-1980s and in subsequent years became a ‘go-to’ destination for revellers from across Greater Manchester, Lancashire and Merseyside In its late-80s and 90s heyday it would host discos, DJs and party nights with a team of bouncers at the door Its large car park and location close to the M61 junction attracted hundreds to the semi-rural pub, many to show of their cars

From neighbourhood pride and climate action to safer streets, better health and stronger communities, the awards recognised the people and organisations putting in the work an More than 900 nominations poured in, shining a light on the extraordinary people doing extraordinary things right on our doorstep. Manchester is packed with people who care, people who act and people who refuse to stand by when they ca Before the big night, nominees were invited to a series of celebratory events at Manchester Town Hall, hosted by the Lord Mayor. candidates.evidence_text: Courts Teenager from Bury admits terror offences over posting of mass killing live stream and murderer's manifesto Damien Woolfenden, 18, appeared at the Old Bailey Add to preferred sources Comments News Andrew Bardsley Court reporter 13:09, 23 Oct 20 A teenager from Bury who posted a video of a mosque shooting and a mass killer’s manifesto has admitted a series of terrorism offences Damien Woolfenden, 18, appeared at the Old Bailey in London to admit 12 offences. They included two offences of disseminating a terrorist publication, including a video of a live stream of mass killings at a mosque in Christchurch, New Zealand by Brenton Tarrant in 2019 A total of 51 people were killed at two mosques in New Zealand. The video was posted onto a self-described 'pro-white' platform on July 22 2025. The second charge related to the posting of the manifesto of mass murderer Anders Breivik Breivik killed 77 people in two attacks in Norway in 2011. Woolfenden posted the manifesto onto a Telegram group in September last year. The defendant also admitted having on his home computer the manifesto of US white supremacist gunman Payton Gendron and the manifesto of German Woolfenden admitted possessing documents on firearms and making bombs. He also published material intending to stir up racial hatred against Jews in posts made on X and on Telegram, as well as material intended to stir up racial hatred against 'foreigners'

candidates.evidence_text: Northenden Pensioner fighting for life after being struck by cyclist on Northenden road Witnesses are being urged to come forward Add to preferred sources News Stephen Topping Senior reporter 11:36, 23 Oct 2026 View 2 Images Police on Palatine road, N A pensioner is fighting for life in hospital after being struck by a cyclist in south Manchester. The 78-year-old man had been walking on Palatine Road, in Northenden , when he was involved in a collision on Thursday (October 22) Greater Manchester Police says it was called out to the scene at 4.30pm. The pedestrian suffered potentially life-threatening injuries and remains in hospital for treatment today (Friday), GMP says The cyclist involved also suffered injuries in the collision. Police say their injuries were not life-threatening No arrests have been made in connection with the incident so far. Multiple officers were seen manning a cordon following the crash on Thursday evening A section of Palatine Road was taped off as police worked at the scene. candidates.evidence_text: Manchester Arndale The 'predatory cash cow' car park in Manchester city centre that has dished out £3.3m in fines Freedom of Information data reveals Manchester City Council dished out more than 66,000 penalty charge notices worth £3.3m at the Arndale Add to preferred sources Comments News John Scheerhout Crime reporter 07:12, 24 Oct 2026 Fines worth more than £3.3 million have been dished out at Manchester's Arndale multi-storey car park in just three years, the Manchester Evening News can reveal The city council took control of the Arndale and other car parks from NCP in 2021, making them barrierless car parks where motorists are supposed to pay on entry either via an app or pay machines But thousands of motorists are being caught out by the new arrangements, which some are dubbing a 'scam' and a 'cash cow' for the council In the 12 months to March 31 this year, some 21,605 motorists were issued a Penalty Charge Notice (PCN) at Manchester Arndale car park which has 1,400 spaces That amounts to PCNs totalling £1,091,430 in one year alone although the actual amount of income coming into the council's coffers will be lower when successful appeals and discounts when the £50 fine is paid promptly

candidates.evidence_text: Manchester Airport Manchester Airport issues October half-term reminder over drop-off and pick-up charges The northern hub is preparing for a busy week ahead, with more than a million passengers expected to pass through its terminals Add to preferred Manchester Airport is preparing to welcome more than a million passengers during the busy October half-term getaway, with bosses issuing key advice to ensure smooth journeys - including a reminder about recent changes to drop-off and pick-up parking operations As families head off for school break holidays, popular sun spots like Alicante , Antalya, Tenerife , and Malaga top the destination list, alongside autumnal city breaks to Derry , Frankfurt, Prague, and Bucharest for Halloween -themed trips With high passenger volumes expected, airport bosses are particularly urging drivers to familiarise themselves with the hub’s updated parking infrastructure to avoid unexpected fines Following last year's introduction of a barrierless forecourt drop-off system , the Terminal 2 West Multi-Storey (P3) now also operates on a barrierless system . Drivers can enter and exit freely without stopping at traditional barriers, helping to cut road congestion around the Non-pre-booked customers using the barrierless drop-off or Terminal 2 West Multi-Storey (P3) areas must pay online or by phone before midnight on the day following their visit

candidates.evidence_text: Trafford Trafford pub wanted 'nightclub hours', but the plan backfired in a way they weren't expecting Bosses were told 'that's the risk' after residents complained about ‘domestics’ and ‘urination' Add to preferred sources Comments News Hannah Richar Bosses at a Trafford pub have been told ‘that’s the risk’ as they lost a bid to stay open later - and instead had new restrictions slapped on their licence Garrick’s Head, in Moorside Road, Flixton, wanted to extend its opening hours to 12.30am on Sundays through Thursdays, 1.30am on Fridays and Saturdays and 2.30am around bank holidays. It also wanted permission to be able to extend opening hours until 2am on up to 20 days each yea But following interventions from neighbours, Trafford council’s licensing committee opted instead to impose a number of new conditions on the pub. Those conditions had been intended by the applicant as safeguards had the extended hours been allowed When the agent speaking on behalf of Garrick's Head questioned the decision, saying the pub had come away with ‘no extra hours’ but ‘more restrictions’, she was told by officers that is ‘the risk that you run when you apply for a variation of the licence’ The decision followed around an hour of representations from residents who labelled the dubbed the proposed changes as ‘nightclub hours’ and said they had been suffering for years. Complaints included disturbed sleep, fights in the street, public urination and littering

The pair, who arrived in the UK by small boat, are accused of trying to acquire components to assemble a homemade explosive device Both men appeared at the Old Bailey in London this afternoon (October 23). Prosecutors allege that the pair were engaging in conduct in preparation for acts of terrorism against the Jewish community in Greater Manchester They were arrested on Newton Street in the Northern Quarter, on September 20, as thousands of British Jews prepared to celebrate the annual occasion. It is alleged that the two men were in contact with an overseas third party who may be in Iran in relation to the plot, Counter Te The defendants appeared in court by video link. They were not asked to enter pleas to the charges they face during the 22 minute hearing, which was presided over by Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb

candidates.evidence_text: Courts Teenager from Bury admits terror offences over posting of mass killing live stream and murderer's manifesto Damien Woolfenden, 18, appeared at the Old Bailey Add to preferred sources Comments News Andrew Bardsley Court reporter 13:09, 23 Oct 20 A teenager from Bury who posted a video of a mosque shooting and a mass killer’s manifesto has admitted a series of terrorism offences Damien Woolfenden, 18, appeared at the Old Bailey in London to admit 12 offences. They included two offences of disseminating a terrorist publication, including a video of a live stream of mass killings at a mosque in Christchurch, New Zealand by Brenton Tarrant in 2019 A total of 51 people were killed at two mosques in New Zealand. The video was posted onto a self-described 'pro-white' platform on July 22 2025. The second charge related to the posting of the manifesto of mass murderer Anders Breivik Breivik killed 77 people in two attacks in Norway in 2011. Woolfenden posted the manifesto onto a Telegram group in September last year. The defendant also admitted having on his home computer the manifesto of US white supremacist gunman Payton Gendron and the manifesto of German Woolfenden admitted possessing documents on firearms and making bombs. He also published material intending to stir up racial hatred against Jews in posts made on X and on Telegram, as well as material intended to stir up racial hatred against 'foreigners'

From neighbourhood pride and climate action to safer streets, better health and stronger communities, the awards recognised the people and organisations putting in the work an More than 900 nominations poured in, shining a light on the extraordinary people doing extraordinary things right on our doorstep. The sheer number of nominations says it all. Manchester is packed with people who care, people who act and people who refuse to stand by when they ca Before the big night, nominees were invited to a series of celebratory events at Manchester Town Hall, hosted by the Lord Mayor. These gatherings gave people the chance to share their stories, celebrate their achievements and recognise the incredible work happening in communities On October 22, the Midland Hotel played host to the inaugural Best of Manchester Awards ceremony, with BBC Radio Manchester's Joe McGrath taking the reins for a night dedicated to the people who make this city what it is

Officers taped off Lord Street, in Cheetham Hill , on Thursday evening (October 23) Greater Manchester Police said a man in his 50s sadly died following a medical episode. It's believed he had been walking in the street at the time of the incident Police attended the scene alongside North West Ambulance Service. evidence_packet.evidence_text: Thursday 15 October 2026 at 7:14pm Play Brightcove video ITV News Granada Reports Correspondent Ann O'Connor was in Bolton Crown Court A former supply teacher who took classroom upskirting photos of schoolgirls and created sexualised deepfake images has been jailed for six years Abusali Rahman, from Salford , used his iPhone to secretly take upskirting images of teenagers while working as a supply teacher in seven high schools in the North West, Bolton Crown Court heard The court heard his victims were 15 girls, all aged between 13 and 16, who were pupils at the different high schools in Bury , Bolton , and Salford Rahman, 37, was only caught when the mother of one girl was scrolling on X and came across an image of her daughter in her school uniform, next to graphic sexual images In other images, he had super-imposed one girl's face on a woman wearing a bikini and another in a PVC suit, the court heard

candidates.evidence_text: Bolton Council is one of at least four local authorities who have refused to accept the government's latest planning changes. Credit: PNW Four local authorities have drawn lines in the sand, refusing to amend their constitutions to adopt the latest statutory government guidance that would see officers become the default body for deciding most planning applications across England Bolton Council, Tameside Council, Central Bedfordshire Council, and Fenland Council have refused to amend their constitutions to be compliant with the National Scheme of Delegation of Planning Functions, which goes into effect on 1 November Their decision will inevitably have consequences, should they continue to refuse to comply In short, the regulation changes mean that more applications will be decided by officers and less by committees This will create a national standard for what is, and what is not, taken to council planning committees – whereas previously local authorities could set their own guidelines for what sort of application merited the committee treatment

Cox was arrested on 14 November 2021 and bailed with stringent bail conditions not to contact the victims On 4 September 2024, a second victim met up with the suspect after again connecting through a dating app. They went to a property in Salford and during that time Cox has taken drugs. Cox then started to remove the victims clothing and blocked the door so she couldn’t leave. Follo Cox was arrested on 8 September 2024, charged and remanded. He stood trial for both rapes in March 2025, however the trial resulted in a hung jury

candidates.evidence_text: How a sweatshop empire is Manchester-washing its reputation “I can’t always be in LA,” reads one TikTok caption, “someone has to hold it down in Rochdale.” It’s written over a model strutting through a leatherwear shoot. She’s wearing Musera, which looks to be Manchester’s friendliest, chicest new clothing label — launched in 2024 from an From this Newton Street office, a band of young designers turn out a stream of trend pieces: low-rise trousers and asymmetric tops, distressed knitwear and leopard-print flares, western fringed jumpers and A-level prom gowns. Their Instagram bio lauds the brand as “Est. MCR.” Over a million people watched the staff dancing around their Northern Quarter office to Whigfield’s Saturday Night on TikTok. More still tuned in to a video showing them kitted out in Musera for Drake’s performance at Co-op Live last year. And who knows how many have sidestepped “Be a muse in your own era,” goes their slogan; presumably also the source of their similarly recondite name. Their Instagram captions are a list of internet cliches verging on parody. “My blood type is iced latte,” reads one post Looking at this well-curated online presence, you might well be convinced that Musera is, as they suggest, Manchester through and through

Many junior staff members believe raising issues will lead to retaliation, and 59% of survey respondents have witnessed or experienced a form of harassment, discrimi One worker recalled a young apprentice being repeatedly sexually harassed by a senior colleague until she was forced to leave the council. “He was allowed to stay,” they said of the offending staffer. “She was interviewed by two male managers and needless to say she left.” There A council worker, speaking to us on the condition of anonymity, said of the report: “if I were a manager that would sicken me to my core.” When we approached the council before publishing this story, CEO Tom Stannard said: “it is completely unacceptable that anyone should feel undervalued, unable to raise concerns, unsupported if they do or – in the worst cases – unsafe. candidates.evidence_text: Police target drivers on busy Timperley road as part of borough-wide "crime-smashing" crackdown Skip to content News — Police, Fire & Court Police target drivers on busy Timperley road as part of borough-wide "crime-smashing" crackdown It was one of several enforcement activities across Trafford. , and David Prior October 23, 2026 . 3:45 PM 2 min read Share on Twitter Share on Facebook Share on Pinterest Share on LinkedIn Share on WhatsApp Share via Email Police carried out a traffic enforcement operation in Timperley yesterday as part of a borough-wide crackdown which resulted in 32 arrests. Officers stopped motorists on Shaftesbury Avenue as part of Operation AVRO, a major Greater Manchester Police initiative which sees additional resources deployed to a different district each month. The traffic operation was one of several enforcement activities carried out across Trafford during the 24-hour operation. Police said more than 50 traffic offence reports were issued overall, including for offences such as failing to wear a seatbelt and using a mobile phone while driving. Two vehicles were seized, while two people were arrested on suspicion of impaired driving and another was arrested for an immigration offence. Greater Manchester Police confirmed that Shaftesbury Avenue was one of the locations used for traffic enforcement. A spokesperson said there was at least one other traffic stop location, although they were unable to confirm exactly where it was. The overall figures also include general traffic stops carried out as part of Operation AVRO, meaning not all the offences or arrests can be attributed to the Shaftesbury Avenue operation. Elsewhere in Trafford, officers carried out a series of early-morning warrants targeting suspected criminal activity. One of the early-morning raids carried out in Trafford yesterday The raids resulted in the recovery of Class A and Class B drugs, while further arrest attempts targeted suspects wanted in connection with ongoing investigations and breaches of court orders. Police also deployed live facial recognition technology and knife arches, alongside targeted patrols and stop-and-search activity. Two arrests were made in the early hours in connection with burglary and going equipped. The operation also included visits to schools and colleges, information stands in town centres, business drop-ins and care home visits. A total of 32 arrests were made during the operation yesterday Chief Superintendent Mike Allen, Trafford district commander, said: "Across the day, officers secured 32 arrests, seized vehicles, recovered drugs, submitted offence reports, and stop-searched suspects across the entire district. "While this is a significant planned day of disruption, I must emphasise that this sort of work is constantly carried out, as officers look to tackle crime and protect our communities." He added that information from residents played an important role in helping police identify suspects and target criminal activity. candidates.evidence_text: Petition against Little Bollington data centre plans passes 1,000 signatures Skip to content News — Environment Petition against Little Bollington data centre plans passes 1,000 signatures Developer Innova wants to build a campus-style data centre on approximately 60 hectares of land south of Lymm Road. , and David Prior October 23, 2026 . 10:50 AM 2 min read Share on Twitter Share on Facebook Share on Pinterest Share on LinkedIn Share on WhatsApp Share via Email A visual showing the proposed data centre in Little Bollington A petition opposing plans for a major new data centre campus in Little Bollington has attracted more than 1,000 signatures. The Change.org petition, titled "Stop the Spode Green Data Centre, Altrincham", had reached 1,047 signatures by this morning. It was launched on October 15 by Lydia Crowther on behalf of the newly formed Spode Green Action Group, which is campaigning against the proposals. Developer Innova wants to build a campus-style data centre on approximately 60 hectares of land south of Lymm Road, north of the M56 and west of the A556. The site, which has an Altrincham postal address but falls within Cheshire East, is owned by the Tatton Estate, which has granted Innova an option to develop the proposals. The scheme has prompted concerns among campaigners about its potential impact on the surrounding countryside. According to the petition, the proposed development would occupy Green Belt land described as "high quality agricultural land" which is currently being actively farmed. Campaigners say the site is equivalent in size to 84 football pitches and that the proposed campus would accommodate eight separate data centres. They also claim early plans indicate an electricity demand of 401 megawatts, which they say would make Spodegreen one of the largest data centre developments in the UK. The petition states: "As a community we are not opposed to development, but these projects should be planned responsibly, and fully consider their long-term effects on both people and the environment." No planning application submitted No planning application has yet been submitted for the development. Innova expects to submit its proposals to Cheshire East Council in late 2026 or early 2027, when they would be subject to the formal planning process. The developer has already held pre-application discussions with council planning officers during 2026. It has also put forward the site for consideration as a strategic employment allocation in Cheshire East's emerging Local Plan. The proposed site of the data centre Developer outlines potential benefits Innova says the project would create around 350 full-time jobs and generate approximately £20 million in additional business rates for Cheshire East Council. Its proposals include a "Living Lab" facility offering training, apprenticeships and opportunities for young people to learn about science, technology, engineering and mathematics. The development would also feature a solar farm and a district heating energy centre, with the potential to capture and reuse waste heat generated by the data centre's servers. Innova describes the proposals as "landscape-led", with existing trees and hedgerows retained and enhanced as part of the development. Further consultation planned Innova held its first public consultation event at High Legh Village Hall on September 30. The company says a second event will take place later this year, when more detailed plans and the findings of environmental surveys will be presented. Residents can submit comments directly to Innova by emailing contact@spodegreendc.com or calling 0800 707 4103. However, comments submitted to the developer at this stage do not constitute formal planning objections. Residents will have an opportunity to make representations to Cheshire East Council if a planning application is submitted. evidence_packet.summary: A public consultation has opened on changes that could affect who secures one of the sought-after grammar school's 204 Year 7 places
evidence_packet.evidence_text: A public consultation has opened on changes that could affect who secures one of the sought-after grammar school's 204 Year 7 places Share on WhatsApp Share via Email Girls living close to Altrincham Grammar School for Girls could lose priority for places to children attending four designated primary schools under proposed changes to its admissions policy A public consultation has opened on plans to give pupils from four primary schools belonging to the same academy trust as AGGS priority over other applicants who have passed the entrance examination – even if they live closer to the school The proposals, which would take effect from September 2028, could have significant implications for Altrincham families whose daughters attend local primary schools outside Bright Futures Educational Trust Under the existing admissions system, girls who pass the entrance examination and live within the school's eight-mile catchment area are generally prioritised according to how close they live to AGGS, after higher-priority categories have been considered But the proposed arrangements would introduce a new category giving preference to qualifying pupils attending four primary schools within Bright Futures Educational Trust

candidates.summary: The site that was once home to Oldham’s sports centre has been given a new lease of life, as the first phase of Tommyfield Park officially opens

candidates.lead: The site that was once home to Oldham’s sports centre has been given a new lease of life, as the first phase of Tommyfield Park officially opens
candidates.evidence_text: First phase of Tommyfield Park officially opens in Oldham town centre | Oldham Council The new Tommyfield Park in Oldham town centre. Published: Friday, 23rd October 2026 The site that was once home to Oldham’s sports centre has been given a new lease of life, as the first phase of Tommyfield Park officially opens. The Mayor of Oldham, Councillor Pam Byrne, marked the occasion with a ribbon cutting on Friday 23 October, celebrating another important milestone in the transformation of Oldham town centre. The first phase of the park covers 1.5 acres, with the completed park set to span 5.7 acres when the second phase opens in 2027. The new park features open lawns, walking trails, seating areas, an amphitheatre-style terrace and space for children and families to play and enjoy the outdoors. It has been designed as somewhere people can relax, meet friends, take a break from the working day or simply enjoy some green space in the heart of the town centre. Tommyfield Park lit up at night in Oldham town centre. The park is a key part of Oldham’s regeneration plans and long-term ambition to create a greener, healthier and more attractive town centre. It will help connect neighbourhoods, support new housing developments and create a welcoming space for residents, workers and visitors to enjoy. It will also link with Snipe Gardens, which opened in June 2025 , helping to create a greener walking route between Oldham Bus Station and the town centre. As well as creating a valuable community space, Tommyfield Park continues the transformation of a site that has played an important role in Oldham’s history. Red sandstone excavated from the site has been incorporated into the landscaping, alongside sections of beech trees from Tandle Hill Country Park, giving a nod to the area’s past while creating a space for future generations. Taking pride of place at the park’s entrance is the Pioneers Stone, created by Frank Rothwell OBE. The stone celebrates Oldham’s role in the birth of the world’s first IVF baby, Louise Joy Brown, at Oldham General Hospital in 1978. It pays tribute to the pioneering medical team, Louise’s parents and the women who helped make the breakthrough possible. The Pioneers Stone, created by Frank Rothwell OBE. Councillor Pam Byrne, Mayor of Oldham said: “This is a proud moment for Oldham. Tommyfield Park is much more than a new park. It’s an investment in our residents, our communities and the future of our town centre. “Creating more green space has been part of our vision for Oldham for many years because we know how important it is for people’s health and wellbeing. “It’s rare to see a major new park created in the heart of a town centre, but as we build new homes and continue to attract investment, it’s important that we create great places for people to enjoy too. “Whether it’s families spending time together, workers taking a break or visitors enjoying our town, this park will become a green heart for Oldham and another example of us delivering on our ambitions for a healthier, happier and greener borough.” The second phase of Tommyfield Park will be built on the site of the former Tommyfield Market Hall and will include a larger play area, climbing features, water play and a sustainable pond. Local young people are also helping to shape the future of the park through engagement with community groups and partners, helping to ensure it remains a safe, welcoming and vibrant space for everyone. Cameron Gates, a young person involved in shaping Tommyfield Park through Spark Oldham said: “Being involved in Tommyfield Park has been a brilliant experience. It’s something that’s going to be here for years to come and knowing I’ve played a part in it makes me really proud. “I’ve been with Spark for two and a half years and it’s made a huge difference to me. I’ve grown so much in confidence, especially with public speaking. I’ve seen Oldham change for the better and in that time I’ve changed a lot too.” Frank Rothwell OBE, Mayor of Oldham Cllr Pam Byrne and Cameron Gates at the new Tommyfield Park. The park has CCTV cameras managed by the council’s First Response team and will be regularly inspected, with town centre maintenance teams helping to keep the space clean and well maintained. candidates.evidence_text: From the fabulous Feast of Fire celebrations to the iconic Christmas Lights Switch-On, the town centre will host an exciting calendar of entertainment as the Greater Manchester Town of Culture 2026 The programme will showcase the very best of Oldham's culture, creativity and community spirit with a series of free family-friendly events The programme begins with the Feast of Fire event on Saturday 31 October 2026. A joint celebration of Halloween and Bonfire Night, this spellbinding event will light up the heart of the town centre with fire dance performances and The Lips Halloween Show by Puppets with Guts foll Then, just two weeks later, the festive season will officially begin with the Oldham Christmas Lights Switch-On event on Saturday 14 November, starting from 1pm. The day will feature meet and greets with Peppa Pig, appearances from Oldham's mascots and activities by the Spindles The celebrations will continue into the evening with the big Switch On Show from 5.30pm featuring Father Christmas, Peppa Pig's Dance Party, Oldham Rock Choir and performances from Fierce Dance The Mayor of Oldham Cllr Pam Byrne will also take part in the celebrations before a local school child competition winner will switch on the town's Christmas lights. The evening will conclude with a festive fireworks finale, accompanied by a lights and laser show

candidates.evidence_text: Wigan Council is introducing new orders to tackle anti-social behaviour in Wigan and Leigh town centres, including targeted powers against e-bikes and scooters These Public Space Protection Orders (PSPOs) will be in place for three years to support the police, council and other authorities in tackling a wide range of issues, reduce crime and help people feel safer in their communities This introduction follows an extensive review of previous orders and a public consultation held over the summer which gathered significant feedback from residents, businesses and the community sector Councillor Kevin Anderson, cabinet portfolio holder for Police, Crime and Civil Contingencies, said: “Residents, businesses and visitors all took part in our consultation, and it was clear that anti-social behaviour remains a concern “Most people who visit, live and work in our town centres do so responsibly, and these orders are aimed at addressing the small number of behaviours that negatively impact our communities, while ensuring support remains available for those who may be vulnerable.” The orders prohibit several anti-social behaviours, with new powers to enforce against anti-social use of cycles, e-bikes and scooters, and drug-related litter and paraphernalia

candidates.evidence_text: Experience the raw, unfiltered power of Balkan folklore in a new immersive show from the world’s most famous performance artist Balkan Erotic Epic is a bold new performance work created by the iconic artist Marina Abramović . Regarded as the world’s most influential performance artist, Abramović’s transformative work has reached millions of people – from opening the Pyramid Stage at Glastonbury Festival t A four-hour ritual where ancient myth meets performance art, Balkan Erotic Epic explores the eroticism, spirituality and traditions of Abramović’s homeland through 13 visceral scenes Brought to life by a cast of over 70 performers, dancers, musicians and singers, the experience unfolds across Aviva Studios. Audiences are free to choose their own path – with pop-up encounters punctuating the action, bringing bodies together in dance, song and ritual Watch Fertility Rite , a fevered ritual where bodies writhe against the ground in a desperate call for fertility. Witness Massaging the Breast where women gesticulate over graves to awaken the earth. In Scaring the Gods , women bare themselves to the sky to banish storms. Listen Unafraid to push the boundaries of eroticism and performance art, Balkan Erotic Epic asks its audience a timeless question: What are our bodies truly for?

History, power and empire collide in Button Up! – a major new exhibition from the world-leading artist and activist Ai Weiwei . Internationally renowned artist and activist Ai Weiwei turns his critical gaze to the last 200 years of global history with this major new exhibition. Monumental in scale and ambition, Ai Weiwei: Button Up! is the artist’s most expansive presentation in the North to date.. Ai Weiwei is known around the world for his uncompromising artistic vision and political activism. From a childhood in exile to surviving secret detention in China, his remarkable life and career have led him to global prominence. Using sculpture, installation, film, photography and architecture, his work is unafraid to ask urgent, critical questions.. In Button Up! , the artist turns his lens on two centuries of Chinese and British relations. Taking inspiration from Manchester, a city at the heart of the Industrial Revolution, Button Up! explores how historic systems of trade, empire and exploitation resonate in today’s humanitarian and political crises.. Conceived as a total environment, Ai Weiwei: Button Up! brings together new and existing large-scale works on display in the UK for the first time. The monumental installation features porcelain, cotton, glass, bronze and even buttons and toy bricks. Each material contains a story of human invention and consumption. Together, they paint a picture of globalisation.. Both global and personal, the title Button Up! is a playful poke at the artist’s ongoing battle with censorship. The exhibition also features the world premiere of a new body of work created especially for the vast spaces of the Warehouse – Eight-Nation Alliance Flags made from millions of buttons, as well as a new version of History Of Bombs made entirely from toy bricks.. The new commissions sit alongside large-scale works by the artist which are going on show in the UK for the first time: Law of the Journey (2017), a 47m long inflatable migrant boat containing hundreds of human figures and the artist’s largest artwork to date; Wang Family Ancestral Hall (2015), a Ming dynasty ancestral temple reassembled from 1,500 individual wooden pieces ; and La Commedia Umana (2017-21), a black Murano glass chandelier made up of over 2,000 pieces and weighing nearly 3 tonnes. Also on show is Circle of Animals/Zodiac Heads (2010), a re-envisioning of the twelve animals of the Chinese zodiac.. Button Up! immerses visitors in Ai Weiwei’s fearless interrogation of the forces past and present that drive today’s injustices – while championing art’s enduring power to challenge and inspire.. . . . “I’m not interested in making very big things just for the sake of it. But in Manchester, that wonderful Warehouse space calls for monumental work. Visiting the city for this exhibition – the birthplace of the Industrial Revolution – and reflecting on Britain’s global territorial expansion made me realise I had to explore that history and understand how it connects to the forces driving today’s wars and global crises. The world today is deeply divided, with tragedy all around. Understanding history goes hand in hand with standing up for truth and justice.”. Ai Weiwei. . . Explore. . Ai Weiwei | Dream Space . It can feel busy and overwhelming without much clarity on what’s actually working. This programme is about helping people step back, put the right foundations in plac The Monthly Marketing Programme is delivered through a structured monthly format, with immediate access to a starter guide on sign-up. candidates.lead: Finish work and unwind with live music from Manchester’s best jazz musicians.
candidates.evidence_text: Finish work and unwind with live music from Manchester’s best jazz musicians. Beat the Jams live series showcases the very best of the jazz scene, at short rush hour gigs from 6pm at Band on the Wall. What better way to avoid those endless queues, chaotic traffic and stressful homeward journeys? Clock off and skip the rush-hour traffic while you watch live jazz and make the most of our happy hour deals from 5–7pm: £4.50 pints / 2 for £15 cocktails / £15 bottles of wine + pizzas from £5! The new season kicks off on 24 September with tenor saxophonist Dean Masser and pianist Richard Wetherall, followed by: 7 October – Anna Chandler-King Quartet Leeds based saxophonist and composer Anna joins us again for Beat the Jams, this time with her own band. Anna’s thoughtful and inventive compositions are firm favourites of us at Beat the Jams and her quartet promises to be a unique rush hour busting treat! 16 November – Sam Lightwing Quartet Saxophonist and composer Sam Lightwing brings presents brand new music for his thrilling young quartet, showcasing Sam’s original compositions, which blend classic mainstream jazz grooves with modern flavours of post-pop and latin, all wrapped up in the language of contemporary sax giants such as Chris Potter, Seamus Blake and Joshua Redman. 15 December – Svarc/Devine/Walsh with Richard Iles The band combines deep pocket, fearless interplay and a shared love of exploration. Expect everything from soulful melodies and infectious rhythms to moments of exhilarating collective improvisation, delivered with the chemistry that only world-class musicians can create. Tickets from £13 per show, or £42 for a season ticket

candidates.evidence_text: We’re inviting young people to explore music for film and compose their own soundtrack this summer! Whether your child already attends our Saturday Music Club, or just wants to try something new, our Young Musician’s Summer School is suitable for all abilities! Across this 5 day course, we’ll be exploring music for film, and working on composing music for the silent film ‘A Trip to the Moon’. The course will conclude with a live performance soundtracking the film for family and friends. We welcome all abilities and instruments to take part in this course. You can bring your own instruments, but we have keyboards, guitars, bass, violins, drums and percussion on site which can be used if you don’t have an instrument. Please email learning@bandonthewall.org if you have any questions about this course

candidates.lead: Mr Thomas’s Chop House has been part of Manchester since 1867.
candidates.evidence_text: Mr Thomas’s Chop House has been part of Manchester since 1867. A £300,000 restoration, long-term lease and 23-year-old head chef are shaping what comes next Go to Manchester's Finest X profile Mr Thomas’s Chop House has been serving Manchester since 1867, but owner Roger Ward admits there was a point after Covid when he wasn’t sure how much longer he wanted to keep doing it Tom’s had gone eight years without a proper lease and much longer without any meaningful investment by the landlord. Retirement was being seriously considered. Instead, Roger decided to “go again properly” That decision has resulted in a new long-term commitment to the Chop Houses and around £300,000 being spent restoring Tom’s – touching everything from the dining rooms and furniture to the menu, wine list, kitchen and beer cellars Roger is particularly pleased with the toilets “Tom’s was famous for the shittest toilets in town,” he says. They are now, by his assessment, considerably less so. Downstairs has been redone, upstairs has new ones too, while a previously overlooked back room has been completely reworked

candidates.evidence_text: The event will bring together more than 20 venues for cocktail takeovers, tastings, collaborations and special events Go to Manchester's Finest X profile Manchester is getting a brand new dedicated cocktail festival this November, with a week-long programme of events taking place across some of the city’s best-known bars Manchester Cocktail Festival will run from Monday 9 to Sunday 15 November, bringing together more than 20 venues for guest bartender appearances, special cocktail menus, tastings, dining experiences and industry events The festival has been created by Nick Coupland of Liar’s Group, the hospitality company behind Crazy Pedro’s, Cane & Grain and Science + Industry, alongside Ben Kendrick of Speak In Code and Double Down Inspired by similar festivals in other UK cities, the pair hope to celebrate Manchester’s cocktail scene while creating opportunities for collaboration between bars, drinks brands and hospitality professionals Participating venues include Speak In Code, Blinker, The Morris, Winsome, Bar Shrimp, Double Down, Stray, Bar Dos, Crazy Pedro’s and Hawksmoor, alongside Northern Quarter favourites Science + Industry, The Daisy and The Bay Horse Tavern

candidates.evidence_text: This year's nominations for Manchester's best bar, best restaurant and best chef are now open Go to Manchester's Finest X profile The Manchester Food and Drink Festival (MFDF) Awards have revealed their 2026 shortlists, with some of Greater Manchester’s best-known restaurants, bars, pubs, cafés and independent food businesses among the nominees The awards ceremony will take place on Monday 25 January 2027, moving to City Hall at Medlock Square for the first time. The new entertainment district is home to a growing collection of bars and restaurants, including Zadie’s and Little Beast Sponsored by Therme Manchester, the awards will recognise businesses and individuals across 17 categories, covering everything from affordable eats and neighbourhood venues to independent producers and the region’s leading chefs Among those competing for Restaurant of the Year are Kallos, Stow, Higher Ground, Winsome, Erst, The Pearl, Adam Reid at The French and The Trof The Chef of the Year shortlist includes Jamie Pickles of Stow, Shaun Moffatt of Winsome, Jess Furniss of WTLGI, Gary Weir of Open Fire and Tartuffe, Sian Wilson of Bar Posie, Tom Barnes of Skof, Rosie Maguire of Higher Ground and Brit Wardle of 10 Tib Lane

The opening marks Open Restaurant Group’s 9th restaurant to date and its second site in Greater Manchester, following the launch of Arcadian in Di At the heart of the restaurant will be a four-to-five-seat chef’s counter, placing guests directly at the pass for an up-close view of the kitchen in action. The interiors will feature four-metre elm trees, curved booth seating and a brass wine display, creating a setting designe Award-winning Andrew Sheridan brings his internationally inspired approach to Counter, building on a career that has seen multiple restaurants under his direction feature in the prestigious Michelin Guide. At Counter, he challenges convention by exploring what British cooking can The menu puts this philosophy into practice with dishes that combine unexpected ingredients and inventive flavour pairings. Highlights include the Beef Tartare Pressed Croissant, pairing aged beef with a crispy pressed croissant, smoked oyster mayo, wasabi and pickled shallot; th From the grill, guests can expect the Satay Spatchcock Chicken, served with peanut satay, fermented chilli, coconut, burnt lime and crispy shallo t, alongside Turbot Steak, a bone-in cut finished with brown butter, green chilli and preserved lemon

The interior showcases the works The famous cocktail menu will return, featuring favourites like the Pink Picante, Pomme Verte – a popular twist on an appletini, Belfast Coffee, the famous spicy pickle martini Especiado and the Pornstar Chic, crafted with homemade passionfruit sorbet Red Light also introduces a brand-new savoury snack menu, including, Boquerones, Pickled Guindilla peppers, Gordal olives, Mini Croissant Butter Blondies from Pollen and homemade Salted Popcorn Ice Cream. To complement the elevated look and taste, Red Light has curated energetic, “Red Light has always been about bringing people together over exceptional drinks in an inviting, unpretentious environment. Our new location gives us the space to realise that vision fully, with the same soul and now a proper home for cocktails, food, and great music.”

They started with UK field sales as a proof of concept initially

candidates.evidence_text: It’s been a busy week at Labour Party Conference in Liverpool, with technology, growth and devolution featuring heavily in many of the conversations we’ve been part of In his first Conference speech as Prime Minister, Andy Burnham talked about devolving more power to places, backing businesses to grow and taking some of what has worked in Greater Manchester into a wider national approach. He also confirmed that AI will be a central focus of the That felt particularly relevant following an event we hosted through the UK Tech Cluster Group with AI Minister Kanishka Narayan, North East Mayor Kim McGuinness and other regional leaders, looking at AI, devolution and local growth One of the clearest themes from the discussion was that devolution should not mean every place trying to build the same thing. Different regions have different strengths, assets and specialisms, and there was a strong view that greater collaboration between places could create bi Procurement and buying local also featured strongly. The discussion highlighted the role public sector buying power can play in supporting regional businesses, helping successful pilots move into commercial contracts and strengthening UK capability in areas such as AI and cyber There was also a broader conversation about sovereignty and the UK’s role internationally. The discussion was not about trying to own every part of the AI stack, but about understanding where the UK already has genuine capability and where it makes sense to build more. Strengths

candidates.lead: Manchester-based charity technology startup Raiser has secured innovation funding and attracted investment from former JustGiving adviser Daryl Upsall as it targets its next phase of growth.
candidates.evidence_text: Raiser wins innovation funding & ex-JustGiving adviser backing Posted on October 23, 2026 by staff Raiser wins innovation funding & ex-JustGiving adviser backing Fundraising technology company strengthens leadership expertise as it develops platform to transform how charities and funders connect Share: Listen to article FinTech Investment Manchester-based charity technology startup Raiser has secured innovation funding and attracted investment from former JustGiving adviser Daryl Upsall as it targets its next phase of growth. The company, which is developing an AI-enabled platform to connect charities with potential funders, has also strengthened its leadership expertise with the addition of experienced figures from the charity, philanthropy and financial sectors. Daryl Upsall, an internationally recognised fundraising consultant who advised JustGiving’s founders during its early development and launch, has joined as an investor and ambassador. Zahra Hedges, former chief executive of Winning Scotland and IoD Director of the Year (Third Sector) 2025, has recently joined as an adviser, while Mark Carrigan, a specialist in philanthropy and capital mobilisation, joined Raiser’s board as a non-executive director earlier this year. The innovation funding, awarded by the GM Business Growth Hub, will support development of Raiser’s grant-matching technology and its wider growth ambitions. Founder 250 star to bring ‘grit, innovation, authenticity’ to FUEL Manchester Founded by former charity leaders, Raiser is developing a technology platform designed to tackle inefficiencies in the charitable funding market by connecting organisations seeking grants with those providing them. While existing fundraising and grant-management platforms typically serve either charities or funders, Raiser is building shared infrastructure for both, allowing charities to capture and communicate their impact while helping funders discover suitable organisations, assess their work and manage funding relationships. The business operates a model that keeps its charity-facing service free, with revenue intended to come from funders using its technology and services. The innovation funding will support development of a grant-matching engine designed to identify suitable funding relationships based on what charities actually do, rather than relying on keywords in grant applications. Built around shared definitions of charitable activities, outcomes and impact, the technology forms part of Raiser’s wider ambition to establish shared data infrastructure for the sector, reducing administrative costs and improving the efficiency of grant-making. Luke Wilkinson is a co-founder of Raiser and a former charity chief executive with 18 years’ experience in the sector. “Right now, small charities lose out for not using the ‘right’ jargon and funders are buried in applications, unclear which charities to back. Meanwhile the quiet grassroots groups doing vital work go unseen. Keyword searches and black-box algorithms don’t fix that,” he said. “We’re building a meaning-based alternative. Every recommendation is explainable, and humans still make the decisions.” The appointments bring significant expertise in fundraising, organisational growth and capital mobilisation to support Raiser’s development. Upsall brings more than 40 years of international fundraising experience, having helped pioneer face-to-face fundraising with Greenpeace International. Hedges more than doubled the annual income of Winning Scotland during her time as chief executive, while Carrigan, managing director of Carrigan Consulting, has advised more than 100 organisations across five continents in raising over $590 million. Beckie Denny, co-founder of Raiser, said: “We’ve built Raiser around a problem we know firsthand from working in the charity sector, but we also see a significant opportunity to change how the wider funding market operates. By creating a platform that serves both charities and funders, we believe we can build a sustainable, scalable business while making charitable funding more accessible and effective. “Securing innovation funding and attracting the support of people with Daryl, Zahra and Mark’s experience is an important step as we develop the technology and work towards the next stage of growth.” Northern Leader Phil McCabe to light up FUEL Manchester Related Stories View All ePayments, once one of UK’s biggest digital payments firms, enters special administration Airtel Mone

candidates.lead: A star of BusinessCloud’s Founder 250 list will discuss the rapid success of his HR tech startup at FUEL Manchester next week.
candidates.evidence_text: Founder 250 star to bring ‘grit, innovation, authenticity’ to FUEL Manchester Posted on October 23, 2026 by Jonathan Symcox Founder 250 star to bring ‘grit, innovation, authenticity’ to FUEL Manchester Tom Keighley to discuss rapid growth of HR tech startup urfuture, recently named fifth most downloaded business app ahead of Zoom Share: Listen to article Founders A star of BusinessCloud’s Founder 250 list will discuss the rapid success of his HR tech startup at FUEL Manchester next week. CEO Tom Keighley (pictured right) co-founded urfuture in Preston in 2024 with COO Jayel Williams (left) and CCO Holly Hobbs (centre). It moved to Manchester at the start of the year before raising £1.7 million in seed investment . The firm is looking to replace CVs and job boards with tech solutions for the AI era. In August, urfuture became the fifth most downloaded business app, ahead of Zoom and just behind Indeed, Teams, LinkedIn and WhatsApp. Keighley, whose work in the talent space dates back to 2011, said the moment meant he “literally had to pause to take it in”. “These are some of the biggest brands in the world with enormous teams, budgets, reach and resources but we have something money can’t buy,” he wrote on LinkedIn. “Grit. Innovation. Authenticity and three incredible individuals who don’t just understand the audience we’re trying to reach, they are that audience.” On Wednesday 28th October, he will speak on the breakfast panel at FUEL Manchester. You can sign up for free at the link below . Register for breakfast panel & networking River Capital led the £1.7m investment, with participation from SyndicateRoom’s Access fund, Manchester Angels, Fhunded, Solid Bond, Host Capital and a number of sector specialist angels. The investment comes as the number of young people aged 16 to 24 not in education, employment or training approaches one million. The problem is being compounded as 45% of job seekers now use AI to help write or edit their CVs, meaning employers are increasingly overwhelmed with high volumes of low-quality, irrelevant applications. The startup is building a new hiring platform that combines a social-first Gen Z distribution engine with a proprietary behavioural science job matching algorithm. This enables employers to identify higher-intent, more diverse candidates and reduce hiring bias, making fairer hiring decisions. Employers including West Midlands Police, Tesco, British Airways and Electricity North West are already using the platform to attract and assess early-career talent. Keighley said: “The UK is rightly focused on how to get more young people earning or learning, but the infrastructure between education and employment is still broken. “CVs don’t work for entry-level talent, job boards don’t reach this generation, and AI has made application volume harder to manage while reducing quality. “We’re rebuilding that system from first principles, combining social distribution, behavioural science and AI to create a fairer, more effective way to connect young people to work. “Our ambition is to become the front door to employment for the next generation.” FUEL Manchester is sponsored by GM Business Growth Hub , S&W and Nybble, with support from Bruntwood SciTech . candidates.evidence_text: A new exhibition at The Portico Library explores feminist themes of wellbeing, ageing and place in relation to magic and ritual healing Open now, Witches & Healers draws on Rosie Reed Hillman’s groundbreaking project Something That Was Ours , which explores what it means to be a witch today Hillman’s portraits of witches and healers are curated in dialogue with historic texts chosen by critical friends who identify with the practice of witchcraft and/or healing. The portraits, the books chosen, and their interpretation offer unique insights into the diverse lives an Using a mix of moving image and photography, the artwork builds a sensory and emotive portrait of women in midlife. Covering themes of menopause, mental health, climate change, and marital breakdown, this work explores the ways women have reclaimed the word witch and sought solac Speaking about the exhibition , Rosie Reed Hillman says: “I have worked to build rapport with contributors over the last four years and believe the intimate access conveyed in this project creates an exhibition that inspires empathy, curiosity and a greater understanding of issue “Women in midlife of all backgrounds are an overlooked demographic who want to see art and hear stories that reflect their experiences, and I hope this work speaks to them especially.”

candidates.lead: Bolton Car Boot Sale at Bolton Car Boot Sale
candidates.evidence_text: Bolton Car Boot Sale is one of the North West's biggest weekly boot sales, held in the hardstanding car park of the Macron Stadium (formerly Reebok), Burnden Way, Horwich, Bolton BL6 6JW. It runs every Sunday from February right through to December, drawing over 300 sellers and thousands of bargain hunters each week. Sellers can arrive and set up from 6:00 AM, with buyers welcomed in from 7:00 AM. Entry costs just £1 per car for buyers. Pitches for sellers are £14 for a car, £20 for a van and £3 for a trailer, with regular and corner pitches available on request. Bring exact change to keep the queue moving, and call organiser Andrew on 07470784644 for more details. Expect hundreds of stalls across the concrete hardstanding pitches, so it goes ahead in most weather. On-site you'll find a 5-star catering service, doughnuts and coffee, ice cream and desserts, a meat auction, fresh fruit and veg, plants, and retro sweet stalls. The sale is dog-friendly, has male and female toilets, ample parking, and kids' rides and bouncy castles to keep little ones entertained. Last confirmed: 10 September 2026 Event date: 2026-10-25 Venue: Bolton Car Boot Sale Price: £1 Status: https://schema.org/EventScheduled

candidates.evidence_text: Football Manchester United Academy Kai Rooney's Man United boost after JJ Gabriel decision and Michael Carrick rule change The son of former United captain Wayne Rooney is being given chances at various levels this season Add to preferred sources Comments Sport Tom Victor 0 Recent developments around JJ Gabriel have given Kai Rooney 's prospects a boost at Manchester United . The son of former skipper Wayne has been getting a taste of action in various age group teams this term and his route into the first team has been made easier thanks to changes Rooney, who turns 17 in November, made his Old Trafford bow in the FA Youth Cup last season. He made his UEFA Youth League debut last week and then scored on his first outing in the Under-18 Premier League this term, opening the scoring in a 1-1 draw with Nottingham Forest The teenager also made his Under-21 debut against Forest, coming on for goalscorer Samuel Lusale in a narrow 3-2 defeat. He's expected to feature this weekend as Darren Fletcher's Under-18s line-up for a huge game against Liverpool Whether he would have received these opportunities with Gabriel ahead of him in the queue is another matter. The wonderkid, who played for the first team in pre-season, hasn't featured since indicating in September that he wanted to leave Old Trafford Get the best United news, updates and analysis straight to your Inbox courtesy of the Manchester Evening News!
